On the second night of the school camp at the forest department hostel, the cook set Vijay's plate on a separate bench by the kitchen door. "You sit here," he muttered, and said something about Vijay's surname.

Vijay, fifteen, sat. His ears burned. Through the doorway he could see the others laughing at the long table. His friend Suraj half-stood, then looked around for a teacher.

Mr D'Souza, the camp in-charge, had seen. He walked over, picked up Vijay's plate, and carried it to the long table himself. "Everyone eats together here. Vijay, sit by me."

Then he went into the kitchen. Nobody heard all of it, but they heard, "This is wrong, and it stops tonight. I'm calling the warden and your supervisor now."

Vijay ate slowly, hands still shaking. Suraj pushed his extra papad onto Vijay's plate without a word.

qa.a: The cook set Vijay's plate on a separate bench by the kitchen door.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling as he sat on the separate bench?
qa.a: Vijay felt humiliated and hurt, ears burning, watching the others laugh together at the long table.

qa.q: What did Mr D'Souza do that was right?
qa.a: He named the exclusion as wrong, brought Vijay to the shared table, and called the warden and the cook's supervisor that same night.

qa.q: What was it like for Suraj to watch it happen?
qa.a: Suraj was upset and unsure what to do alone, looking for a teacher, and then quietly showed support with his papad.

grounding: Shows a teenager made to eat separately because of his background, the hurt it causes, and an adult naming it wrong and acting at once.

Dear Tsering,

Something happened at our class potluck today, and I need to tell someone who'll get it.

One of the parents organising it put a sign on a table in the corridor: "Non-veg tiffins here." So Aslam, two others and I ate outside while everyone else was in the classroom. I had brought Amala's momos. I felt like the food was dirty, and so was I.

Then Rukmini ma'am came out. She looked at the sign for a second, took it down, and said, "Nobody eats in a corridor in my class. That isn't a food rule, that's leaving people out, and it's wrong." She carried our tiffins inside, put separate serving spoons on every dish, and made a veg side and a non-veg side on the same long table.

After the bell I saw her talking to that parent, calmly, for a long time.

Two girls asked for my momo recipe.

Pema

qa.a: Pema felt ashamed and hurt, as if both the food and Pema were dirty.

Promise you won't make it a big thing? Okay. I'm Mahima, I've lived next door to Uma my whole life, and until this year I went to every puja at her house.

This time Uma's Dadi was visiting from the village. When I came to the door, she stopped me. "Your people eat outside," she said, and pointed to the steps. I didn't even understand at first. Then I did.

I went home and sat in the bathroom so Mummy wouldn't see my face.

An hour later Uma's mother knocked on our door. She'd heard from Uma. She said to Mummy and me, "What happened was wrong. It won't happen in my home again. I've told Mummyji so." Then she asked me to come back and eat with them, at the table, next to Uma.

I went. Dadi didn't speak to me. But Uma held my hand under the table the whole time.

I'm Hafsa, and last Diwali I learned how complicated one plate can be.

Tejas and I have eaten from the same mess tray for two years. He's vegetarian; I eat only halal. In the hostel we just work around it: I skip the meat curry when it isn't halal, he skips the eggs, and we share everything else.

So when he invited me home to Nashik for Diwali, I didn't think about food at all. His mother cooked a feast, all vegetarian, which I loved. But she served me on a separate steel plate kept on a high shelf, and later I saw her wash it apart from the others.

I felt it in my stomach, a small cold drop.

On the train back I told Tejas. He went red. "I didn't know she still did that. It's not right. I'll talk to her."

I told him I'm happy to eat vegetarian in his home forever. The separate plate is the part I can't pretend not to see.

Warden's note, Girls' Hostel Block C, 14 March

There was tension in the common kitchen this week. A first-year complained that Maria's beef fry was in the same fridge as her vegetarian tiffin and called it "disgusting". Maria cried.

Hafsa, a second-year who is fasting for Ramzan, came to me the same evening with a plan: separate labelled shelves by diet, lids on everything, and one rule written at the top: "Respect every restriction. Nobody's food is dirty."

She said, "I don't eat pork, and I'd hate it touching my food. But I'd hate even more being called disgusting."

What I did next: I put up her notice, sat the three of them down together, and asked the first-year to apologise for the word, not the preference. She did. On Friday, Maria waited until sunset to eat so she could break the fast with Hafsa.

At her housewarming in the new Chennai flat, Gopika had cooked the way her grandmother did: a full vegetarian meal, sambar, three poriyals, payasam. Her kitchen would stay vegetarian; that part mattered to her.

Then Nitin arrived, beaming, with a large box. "Chicken biryani from the best place in Triplicane!"

Two of her cousins exchanged a look.

Gopika hesitated only a second. "Thank you, Nitin, that's so kind." She set up a small table on the balcony with its own plates and serving spoon. "Biryani lovers, this way. Sambar lovers, that way. Both, both."

Everyone laughed. When a cousin muttered something about the smell in the house, Gopika said lightly, "Nobody's plate is up for comments today, Anna."

By evening the biryani box and the payasam pot were both empty.

Dear Biji,

Thank you for the weekend in Jalandhar. I'm writing because of Sunday lunch.

You kept putting rotis on my plate, and at the fourth I put my hand over it and said, "Bas, Biji." I saw your face drop for a second, and you went quietly back to the tawa. Baljeet told me later you'd asked him whether I didn't like your cooking.

I was so sorry. I understand now: every roti was your way of saying welcome. In my family in Mangalore, love comes as endless questions; in yours, it comes hot off the tawa.

So let me say it in words: your makki roti was the best thing I've eaten this year. I stopped at three only because I was full. Next time I'll come hungry, have one more, and then ask you to teach me.

With love,
Chandrika

So you asked how Dev's first lunch at my parents' went. I'm Ankita, and I have never watched anyone eat so nervously.

My mother, Vasudha, had cooked for two days. She kept sliding pooris onto his plate, one after another, and Dev kept saying, "No, Aunty, really, I'm full," in his polite way. By the sixth no, her smile had gone stiff. She went into the kitchen and banged a vessel.

I followed Dev to the balcony and explained. "In our house, food is how she says she likes you. When you refuse, she hears that you don't like her."

He looked horrified. He went straight back in, took one more poori, and said, "Aunty, this is the best aloo I've ever had. Can I take some home? I can't eat another bite now, but I don't want to miss it."

She packed him a tiffin big enough for a week. That's how I knew he was in.

Periamma laughed, a real laugh. Hemant took one more small spoon of payasam, eyes closed as if it were heaven.

I was nine, in a village near Amritsar. My best friend Harjeet dragged me to the fields on Baisakhi morning. The wheat was gold and everyone was singing. I asked his Bapu, "Why dance for wheat?"

Hi Kamal bhaiya,

Diwali report from Indore, as promised.

Week one: cleaned the whole house, including the loft, which had a dead lizard in it. Week two: made four hundred shakkarpara with Mummy and Nani. Diwali day: visited eleven relatives' houses. Eleven. I said "Happy Diwali, Aunty" so many times my jaw hurts.

I'd wanted just one day to sleep and go to Nishant's to try his new game. Every time I asked, it was "After Bhai Dooj."

So on Thursday I asked properly, at breakfast. "Mummy, I'll do all the visits tomorrow without complaining, but can I have Saturday off?" She said yes. I think she was shocked I asked nicely.

Weird part: at the last house, Dadi's old friend gave me the same besan laddoo she gave me when I was five, and I nearly cried. I don't know why.

Miss you at these things. Send photos of your Toronto Diwali.

Sachin
